assumptions: Every committed element costs one Goldilocks symbol in the Ligero tableau (rows = ceil(elements/l), n symbols per row):a hash-based PCS has no cheap small-value or 0/1 commitments, which is what Lasso/Shout's savings rest on.

Grand products (Lasso memory checking, plookup) are proved by Thaler's product-tree GKR; its sequential chain has the samelayer structure as the fractional GKR (k-variable degree-3 sumcheck + one 2-to-1 message per layer).

Extra chunk digits of a range check split into more chunks than the 16-bit convention are committed hint columns (A) /slots (B); the 16-bit baseline's own chunk digits are inside the census's 321 committed columns (delta accounting).

Lasso's primary sumcheck has degree 2 (range decomposition g is linear); its 4c grand products, the primary sumcheck andthe fixed tables' fractional GKRs run in parallel; sharding splits N and duplicates the counters.
Shout: read-checking (log N + 16 rounds), booleanity and Hamming-weight-one sumchecks in parallel; no tree, so shardingdoes not apply; field ops (d+2) per committed one-hot element.

One logUp over all tables folds the public table id into the beta-compression of the row (no committed selector: the idis fixed per query position by the circuit); the beta-degree term is charged at the widest table (4 columns).
The checker's layer shape (DEFAULT_LAYERS_A) is left unchanged under every option: the extra split identities are< 1% of the assertion layer width and do not change its log2 size.

Non-logUp options add their argument additively to the accountant's checker + fixed-tables figure with the accountant'sown constants (EXT_MULT_COST, _ntt_ops, 15 F_c mults per tree leaf); their soundness terms are Schwartz-Zippel of theproduct degree over F_c (same order as the logUp identity).
Candidate B has no sumcheck: a grand product there is a committed running-product column (L F_c elements), so Lasso andplookup in B are priced as committed cells; Shout in B is not applicable.
summary: Killing question: no option beats logUp on both committed elements and depth for Candidate A at any B, and none beats logUp-16 on committed cells for Candidate B at B >= 64.  LogUp with fractional GKR is committed-optimal (multiplicities only); every argument that avoids the quadratic-depth tree (Shout) or changes the tree (Lasso, plookup) commits O(N) or O(N M^(1/d)) extra elements, x4.7 (Lasso c=2) to x40 (Shout d=4) at B=4096.

Depth lever inside logUp: dedicated T_range7/8/9 tables move 128 of the 284 range queries per unit off T_range16 (N: 111.7M -> 61.3M, hypercube 27 -> 26): depth 381 -> 354 at B=4096 for +9.2k committed elements (+0.005%); with the c=2 / s=5 proposals both sit on the checker-chain floor (158), so the lever is worth 27 trips only if the proposals are not adopted.

Table width: 16-bit chunks are optimal for B at B >= 4 (every 16 < w <= 32 check is two chunks whatever W in 16..22; narrower chunks add 127-175 queries and 127-175 digit columns per unit).  At B = 1 (U = 96) the 65 536 multiplicity rows dominate: 8/12-bit chunks halve A's and B's committed elements (116k -> 67k; 457k -> 260k) at equal depth (checker chain 225 is the floor); crossover B ~ 3 (8-bit) / ~ 4 (12-bit).

Fixed tables (ALIGN/POW/LEAD/NORM, <= 512 rows, 22 queries per unit) need no Lasso: their logUp trees have dimension 20-23 at B=4096 (chains 210-276, under the checker chain 297); their multiplicity vectors total 1 087 elements.

One logUp over all tables (public table id in the row compression) is depth-neutral (hypercube 27 either way) and saves only the four extra trees' pads (-8.4k committed, -0.1 MB transcript at B=4096) at the price of a single challenge z for all tables; one grand product per table (plookup) costs +N+|T| committed per table (+112M at B=4096) at equal depth.
cq-like multiplicity-free lookups are excluded: they need a pairing-based KZG commitment to the table (hash-based only).
